fields.v: Chen, V., Talwalkar, A., Brennan, R., Neubig, G. (2026). Code with Me or for Me? How Increasing AI Automation Transforms Developer Workflows. In: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26), ACM. https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3790850. Read from arXiv:2507.08149v2 [cs.SE], 13 Sep 2025
Conference — CHI 2026 (ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems), DOI 10.1145/3772318.3790850 (venue from the ACM/WoS exports); full text read from arXiv:2507.08149v2
Carnegie Mellon University (Chen, Talwalkar, Neubig); All Hands AI (Chen, Brennan, Neubig), the company behind OpenHands, the agent evaluated
Compares — controlled within-participant user study (20 developers) of a coding copilot (GitHub Copilot) vs a coding agent (OpenHands) on productivity, user experience and interaction patterns
No SDD approach. Tools compared: GitHub Copilot (copilot baseline; autocomplete plus chat with ask/edit/agent modes; version not stated) and OpenHands (coding agent, web app, versions 0.35-0.38)
N/A (no approach prescribing artefacts). Participants received a task description (instructions.txt) and starter repository per task; final code pushed to a GitHub repository
Not prescribed. Observed workflow steps (Fig. 5): implement functionality, environment set-up, debug implementation; with the agent, set-up and debugging shift to the AI

Not prescribed by an approach. Copilot: edit and agent mode proposals must be accepted by the user; OpenHands: acts autonomously, the user inspects outputs and sends new instructions between agent turns
Full interactive use of each tool by participants (40 min per condition); no SDD approach exercised
Not classifiable (no specification-driven approach; authors do not use SDD terms)
Both: data analysis programs from scratch (GAIA, extended) and existing code bases (add feature to matplotlib; fix bugs in scikit-learn and astropy, from SWE-Bench)

6 tasks (2 per type: data analysis, add feature, fix bug); 20 participants; 40 min per condition, about 90 min total per participant. Repository sizes Not stated (real-world libraries matplotlib, scikit-learn, astropy)
Python scientific/data libraries (matplotlib, scikit-learn, astropy) and web data analysis (home sales, TV show statistics)

20 students recruited via university mailing lists, working individually; regular GitHub Copilot users (at least weekly), no prior coding-agent experience; 60% 3-5 years professional programming experience, 25% 0-2, 15% 6-10; 95% intermediate to advanced Python
No tokens or money. Time: agent condition total time including agent actions averaged 27.9 min (reported in text, not a planned metric)
Task correctness rate: whether the final code satisfies all task specifications
None

User effort time for correctly solved tasks (copilot: total time start to end; agent: sum of time between the agent's last action before a user message and its first action after it, i.e. inspecting and writing instructions). Likert ratings incl. cognitive load

User experience: 5-point Likert ratings on 6 comparison statements (cognitive load, new tasks, speed, flow, satisfaction, understanding of outputs) and 2 future-usage statements; qualitative survey answers; interaction trajectories (exploratory)

Automatic: OpenHands event stream telemetry (time). Manual: copilot screen recordings coded manually; final code snapshots pushed to GitHub and judged for correctness (grader and procedure not described); post-study Google form (Likert, open-ended). Analysis: linear model with condition and problem as fixed effects (alpha 0.05); Wilcoxon signed-rank test of Likert medians against neutral 3

(1) Baseline: GitHub Copilot (version not stated) + participant-chosen LLM (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 3.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro or o3-mini) + human participant. Success criterion: per task, code satisfies all task specifications; no criterion stated by the authors for the configuration. Values: task correctness mean 25% (SE 10%); user effort 25.1 min (SE 6.22) on correct solutions. Quality verdict: no criterion stated by the authors. Cost verdict: no criterion stated by the authors. (2) OpenHands 0.35-0.38 + Claude Sonnet 3.7 + human participant. Success criterion: same per-task criterion; no criterion stated for the configuration. Values: task correctness mean 60% (SE 11%); user effort 12.5 min (SE 2.8); total including agent action time about 27.9 min. Quality verdict: no criterion stated by the authors. Cost verdict: no criterion stated by the authors

Tasks: 6 realistic tasks (2 GAIA data analysis, extended; 2 matplotlib feature additions written by the authors; 2 SWE-Bench bug fixes); the 4 GAIA and SWE-Bench tasks chosen as unsolved by OpenHands alone in a previous evaluation. Configurations: GitHub Copilot vs OpenHands. Baseline: GitHub Copilot. Held constant: participant (within-participant), task type (same type in both phases, type assigned between-subjects), time limit 40 min per condition, task instructions; order randomized. Not held constant: LLM (free choice in Copilot, fixed Claude Sonnet 3.7 in OpenHands); environment (own IDE vs hosted web app). Acceptance: correctness against task specifications (no tests described). Repetitions: one session per participant per condition (n = 20), asynchronous. Human intervention: inherent (interactive use); $35 compensation based on effort, not correctness
fields.why: The draft said all 6 tasks were chosen as unsolved by OpenHands alone; Appendix B states this only for the GAIA and SWE-Bench tasks (p. 22, 24); the matplotlib tasks were created by the authors (p. 25)

fields.v: Agent better on correctness: 60% vs 25% (+35 percentage points, p = 0.02); agent lower user effort on correct solutions: 12.5 vs 25.1 min (p = 0.01), but total time with agent actions (27.9 min) comparable. No significant difference between task types. Likert: agents preferred for accomplishing new tasks (p = 0.0013) and less cognitive load (p = 0.0006); no significant difference for speed (p = 0.09), flow (p = 0.39), satisfaction (p = 0.26); better understanding of copilot outputs (55%, p = 0.07). OpenHands rated more competent than a human programmer (p = 0.002), yet participants would continue to prefer GitHub Copilot (p = 0.04)

Distinguished the two tools on correctness and user effort with significant differences; single session per participant, not repeated. Limitations stated: one instance of each tool type; LLM not controlled in the copilot condition; mostly student participants, novice agent users; limited number of tasks; time measurement may not be representative (no multitasking, short sessions); tasks pre-defined, no planning; findings tied to April-May 2025

Limitations: one copilot and one agent; copilot LLM not controlled; student participants with no agent experience; few, short tasks not representative of multi-day work; time measure may not be representative; popular languages/packages only; planning not covered; point-in-time results. Gaps: agent transparency (explanations of actions), balanced proactivity (when to stop, resource control), better use of human effort (latency, steering, multitasking/mixed-initiative workflows); effect of different LLM backbones; power users

Inconsistencies: abstract and text say '35% increase in task correctness', which is percentage points (25% to 60%) (p. 2, 9); p. 9 lists '(µ = 25% ... compared to µ = 60% ... respectively)' after naming agents first, order inferred from 'increase'; text labels C1 = new tasks and C2 = cognitive load (p. 11) while Table 2 has C1 = cognitive load and C2 = new tasks (p. 10); Table 3 F2 reads 'continue to use OpenHands over Github Copilot' (p. 13) while the survey item reads 'continue to use Github Copilot over OpenHands' (p. 28); text says all participants used GitHub Copilot at least once a week (p. 5) while Figs. 8-9 have a category 'Used to use Github Copilot, not currently use anymore' (p. 28-29); Copilot's own agent mode was available to participants (p. 21) and its use is not reported. Effort measured differently for the two conditions (p. 8-9). Correctness values only in Fig. 4 and text. Analysis scripts at https://github.com/valeriechen/copilot-agent-comparison (p. 9); screen recordings not released (p. 27). No pre-registration. Programming language: Python
fields.why: Missing inconsistency added: participants said to be weekly Copilot users (p. 5) vs a 'no longer use Copilot' category in Figs. 8-9 (p. 28-29)
